subject: maths
title: Money: Coins, Notes, Counting and Giving Change
seo_title: Year 2 Money Worksheets: Australian Coins, Notes and Change
standard_text: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical additive and multiplicative problems, including money transactions, representing the situation and choosing calculation strategies; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
meta_desc: Free Year 2 maths worksheets on money: name and order Australian coins and notes, count collections of cents and dollars, make 50c or $10 in different ways, give change from $1, $2 and $5 by counting on, and solve school canteen shopping problems. 100 questions with an answer key, following the Australian Curriculum.
key_big: Read the number on each coin, then count on from the biggest.
key_sub: Size is not value: the 50c coin is the biggest, and the small $2 coin is worth more than the $1 coin. $1 = 100c. To give change, count on from the price: 35c to 40c to $1 is 5c + 60c = 65c.
body_html:
Coins and notes

We write cents with a small c: 50c. We write dollars with the $ sign in front: $5. $1 is the same as 100c.

A big coin is not always worth more. The 50c coin is the biggest coin. The $2 coin is smaller than the $1 coin, but it is worth more. Always read the number.

Count the money, biggest first

Put the coins in order. Start with the biggest value and count on.

Example

Count $10, $5 and $2.

Start with the note worth the most: $10, $15, $17.

Answer: $17

Make an amount in different ways

50c can be 20c + 20c + 10c, or 10c + 10c + 10c + 10c + 10c, or one 50c coin. For the fewest coins, use the biggest coin you can each time.

Example

Find two ways to make 30c.

20c + 10c = 30c. 10c + 10c + 10c = 30c. 20c + 10c uses the fewest coins.

Answer: 20c + 10c or 10c + 10c + 10c

Give change by counting on

Start at the price. Count on to the money you paid. The jumps are the change.

Example

A sushi roll costs $4. You pay with a $5 note. What is the change?

Count on: $4 + $1 = $5.

Answer: $1

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
4 coins, so 4cCount the value of each coin: 50c, 70c, 80c, 85c
The 50c coin is the biggest, so it is worth the mostRead the number: $1 and $2 are worth more
The $1 coin is bigger than the $2 coin, so it is worth more$2 is two dollars. Size does not tell you the value
$5 is the same as 5c$5 is five dollars. $1 alone is 100c
Change from $1 for 35c is 75cCount on: 35c + 5c = 40c, 40c + 60c = 100c. The change is 65c

faq.q: What do Year 2 students learn about money in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: In Year 2 (AC9M2N06), students count collections of coins and notes, make the same amount in different ways and solve simple shopping problems, such as working out change from $1, $2 or $5.

faq.q: Is the $2 coin bigger than the $1 coin?
faq.a: No. The $2 coin is smaller than the $1 coin, but it is worth more. The 12-sided 50c coin is the biggest Australian coin, so size never tells you the value.

faq.q: How do you teach a Year 2 child to give change?
faq.a: Count on from the price to the money paid. For 35c paid with $1: 35c to 40c is 5c, 40c to 100c is 60c, so the change is 65c.

faq.q: Why does my child say 4 coins make 4c?
faq.a: Young children often count the coins instead of their value. Ask them to read the number on each coin, put the coins in order from biggest value and count on: 50c, 70c, 80c, 85c.

items.q: How much is this coin worth?
items.e: The coin says 5c. The c means cents. It is worth 5c, our smallest coin.

items.q: How much is this coin worth?
items.e: The coin says 20c. It is worth 20c (20 cents). $20 is a note.

items.q: How much is this coin worth?
items.e: This 12-sided coin says 50c. It is worth 50c (50 cents). There is no $50 coin.

items.q: How much is this gold coin worth?
items.e: This gold coin is $1 (one dollar). $1 is worth 100c.

items.q: How much is this gold coin worth?
items.e: This small gold coin is $2 (two dollars). It is not 20c.

items.q: How much is this note worth?
items.e: This note says $5. It is worth $5 (five dollars).

items.q: How much is this note worth?
items.e: This note says $10. It is worth $10 (ten dollars).

items.q: How do you write 20 cents?
items.e: Write the number, then c for cents: 20c. $20 would be 20 dollars.

items.q: How do you write 5 dollars?
items.e: Write the $ sign first, then the number: $5. 5c would be 5 cents.

items.q: How many cents make $1?
items.e: $1 = 100c. Two 50c coins or ten 10c coins make $1.

items.q: Which coin is worth the most?
items.e: The $2 coin is worth the most, even though it is one of the smallest coins. The 50c coin is the biggest, but it is only worth 50 cents. Read the number, not the size.

items.q: Which coin is worth the least?
items.e: The smallest number is 5. The 5c coin is worth the least.

items.q: The $1 coin is bigger than the $2 coin. Which coin is worth more?
items.e: Size does not tell you the value. $2 is more than $1, so the $2 coin is worth more.

items.q: The 50c coin is bigger than the $1 coin. Which coin is worth more?
items.e: $1 = 100c, and 100c is more than 50c. So the $1 coin is worth more, even though it is smaller.

items.q: Which coin has 12 sides?
items.e: The 50c coin has 12 sides. All the other coins are round.

items.q: Which of these is a note?
items.e: Notes are made of plastic: $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100. $10 is a note. $1 and $2 are coins.

items.q: Which is worth more: 50c or $1?
items.e: $1 = 100c. 100c is more than 50c, so $1 is worth more.

items.q: Which coin is worth the same as two 50c coins?
items.e: 50c + 50c = 100c = $1. Two 50c coins are worth the same as one $1 coin.

items.q: Put these coins in order. Start with the least.
items.e: Cents come first: 20c is less than 50c. Then dollars: $1, then $2. Order: 20c, 50c, $1, $2. Do not order them by size.

items.q: Put this money in order. Start with the most.
items.e: The biggest number is worth the most: $20, $10, $5, $2.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each coin is 10c. Count in 10s: 10c, 20c, 30c, 40c. That is 40c. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins.

items.q: Liam has these coins. How much does he have?
items.e: Each coin is 5c. Count in 5s: 5c, 10c, 15c, 20c, 25c, 30c. That is 30c. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins.

items.q: William finds these coins in his pencil case. How much is it?
items.e: Each coin is 20c. Count in 20s: 20c, 40c, 60c. That is 60c. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins.

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 10c, 20c, 25c. That is 25c.

items.q: Mia puts this money in her money box. How much is in the box?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 20c, 30c, 35c. That is 35c.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each coin is 20c. Count in 20s: 20c, 40c, 60c, 80c. That is 80c.

items.q: Harper has these coins. How much does she have?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 50c, 60c, 70c. That is 70c.

items.q: Amelia finds these coins in her pencil case. How much is it?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 20c, 40c, 45c. That is 45c.

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 50c, 70c, 90c. That is 90c.

items.q: Ruby puts this money in her money box. How much is in the box?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 50c, 70c, 75c. That is 75c.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Put the money in order, biggest first. Start with the biggest coin and count on: 20c, 40c, 50c, 55c. That is 55c.

items.q: Jack has these coins. How much does he have?
items.e: Put the money in order, biggest first. Start with the biggest coin and count on: 50c, 55c, 60c, 65c. That is 65c.

items.q: Ava finds these coins in her pencil case. How much is it?
items.e: Put the money in order, biggest first. Start with the biggest coin and count on: 50c, 70c, 80c, 85c. That is 85c.
Each coin is 50c. Count in 50s: 50c, 100c. 100c = $1. $2 counts each 50c coin as $1.

items.q: Chloe puts this money in her money box. How much is in the box?
items.e: Each coin is $1. Count in 1s: $1, $2, $3. That is $3. Dollars are not cents: $3 is not 3c.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each coin is $2. Count in 2s: $2, $4, $6. That is $6. Dollars are not cents: $6 is not 6c.

items.q: Cooper has these coins. How much does he have?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: $2, $4, $5. That is $5. Dollars are not cents: $5 is not 5c.

items.q: Mei puts this money in her money box. How much is in the box?
items.e: Put the money in order, biggest first. Start with the biggest note and count on: $5, $7, $8. That is $8. Dollars are not cents: $8 is not 8c.

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Start with the biggest note and count on: $10, $15, $17. That is $17. Dollars are not cents: $17 is not 17c.

items.q: Sienna puts this money in her money box. How much is in the box?
items.e: Put the money in order, biggest first. Start with the biggest note and count on: $10, $15, $17, $18. That is $18. Dollars are not cents: $18 is not 18c.

sets.title: Make an amount in different ways

items.q: Which coins make 30c?
Which coins make 50c?
Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 20c, 40c, 50c. That is 50c. So one 50c coin is worth the same.

items.q: Which coins make $1?
Which of these does not make 40c?
items.e: 20c + 10c + 5c = 35c, not 40c. The others all make 40c.

items.q: What is the fewest coins you can use to make 60c?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 50c + 10c = 60c. That is 2 coins. There is no 60c coin, so 1 coin is not possible. Six 10c coins also make 60c, but that is more coins.

items.q: Lachlan has 3 coins. Together they make 45c. Which coins does he have?
Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Each coin is $1. Count in 1s: $1, $2. That is $2. So one $2 coin is worth the same.

items.q: Which coins make 75c?
Which uses the fewest coins to make 70c?
items.e: All of these make 70c. 50c + 20c uses only 2 coins. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: What is the fewest coins you can use to make 90c?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: 50c + 20c + 20c = 90c. That is 3 coins. Two coins cannot make 90c: 50c + 50c = $1 is too much.

items.q: Which is worth the same as this money?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: $2, $4, $5. That is $5. So one $5 note is worth the same.

items.q: Which make $10?
Which make $15?
Kai has 4 coins. Together they make 80c. Which coins does he have?
Which of these does not make $1?
items.e: 50c + 20c + 20c + 5c = 95c, not $1. The others all make $1.

items.q: What is the fewest coins and notes you can use to make $8?
items.e: Use the biggest one you can each time: $5 + $2 + $1 = $8. That is 3 coins and notes. No two of them make $8 ($5 + $2 = $7, $5 + $5 = $10). Eight $1 coins also make $8, but that is a lot.

items.q: Which of these does not make $5?
items.e: $2 + $2 + $2 = $6, not $5. The others all make $5.

items.q: Which make $12?
Which coins make 95c?
Charlotte buys a ruler for 90c. She pays with a $1 coin. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count on from 90c to $1: 90c + 10c = $1. The change is 10c. Check: 90c + 10c = $1.

items.q: Leo buys a balloon for 80c. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from 80c to $1: 80c + 20c = $1. The change is 20c. Check: 80c + 20c = $1.

items.q: Oliver buys a bag of popcorn for 50c. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count on from 50c to $1: 50c + 50c = $1. The change is 50c. Check: 50c + 50c = $1.

items.q: Liam buys an eraser for 70c. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from 70c to $1: 70c + 30c = $1. The change is 30c. Check: 70c + 30c = $1.

items.q: William buys a cheese stick for 60c. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count on from 60c to $1: 60c + 40c = $1. The change is 40c. Check: 60c + 40c = $1.

items.q: Grace buys an apple for 40c. She pays with a $1 coin. How much change does she get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from 40c to $1: 40c + 60c = $1. The change is 60c. Check: 40c + 60c = $1.

items.q: Mia buys a pen for $1. She pays with a $2 coin. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count on from $1 to $2: $1 + $1 = $2. The change is $1. Check: $1 + $1 = $2.

items.q: Zara buys a sausage roll for $3. She pays with a $5 note. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count on from $3 to $5: $3 + $2 = $5. The change is $2. Check: $3 + $2 = $5.

items.q: Harper buys a sushi roll for $4. She pays with a $5 note. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count on from $4 to $5: $4 + $1 = $5. The change is $1. Check: $4 + $1 = $5.

items.q: Amelia buys a drink for $2. She pays with a $5 note. How much change does she get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from $2 to $5: $2 + $3 = $5. The change is $3. Check: $2 + $3 = $5.

items.q: Noah buys a pen for $1. He pays with a $5 note. How much change does he get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from $1 to $5: $1 + $4 = $5. The change is $4. Check: $1 + $4 = $5.

items.q: Ruby buys a party hat for 95c. She pays with a $1 coin. How much change does she get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from 95c to $1: 95c + 5c = $1. The change is 5c. Check: 95c + 5c = $1.

items.q: Ethan buys a fruit cup for 75c. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count on from 75c to $1: 75c + 5c = 80c, 80c + 20c = $1. Add the jumps: 5c + 20c = 25c. The change is 25c. Check: 75c + 25c = $1.

items.q: Jack buys a pencil for 45c. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from 45c to $1: 45c + 5c = 50c, 50c + 50c = $1. Add the jumps: 5c + 50c = 55c. The change is 55c. Check: 45c + 55c = $1.

items.q: Ava buys a sticker for 35c. She pays with a $1 coin. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count on from 35c to $1: 35c + 5c = 40c, 40c + 60c = $1. Add the jumps: 5c + 60c = 65c. The change is 65c. Check: 35c + 65c = $1.

items.q: Matilda buys a bookmark for 85c. She pays with a $1 coin. How much change does she get? Count on along the number line.
items.e: Count on from 85c to $1: 85c + 5c = 90c, 90c + 10c = $1. Add the jumps: 5c + 10c = 15c. The change is 15c. Check: 85c + 15c = $1.

items.q: Chloe buys an eraser for 70c. She pays with a $1 coin. Which coins could she get as change?
items.e: $1 = 100c. Count on from 70c to 100c: 30c. 20c + 10c = 30c, so 20c, 10c. 20c + 20c = 40c is too much.

items.q: Aarav buys a pencil for 45c. He pays with a $1 coin. Which coins could he get as change?
items.e: Count on from 45c: 45c + 5c = 50c, 50c + 50c = 100c. The change is 55c. 50c + 5c = 55c, so 50c, 5c.

items.q: Cooper pays with a $1 coin and gets 30c change. How much did he spend?
items.e: Count on from 30c to 100c: 30c + 70c = 100c. He spent 70c. Check: 70c + 30c = 100c = $1.

items.q: Mei pays with a $5 note and gets $2 change. How much did she spend?
items.e: $2 + $3 = $5, so she spent $3. $7 adds the change instead of taking it away.

items.q: Isla buys an apple and popcorn. How much does she spend?
items.e: 30c + 50c: 3 tens + 5 tens = 8 tens. That is 80c. 20c is the difference, not the total. 35c just puts the 3 and the 5 together.

items.q: Sienna buys 2 bags of popcorn. How much does she spend?
Lachlan orders a pie and a juice. How much does it cost?
items.e: $5 + $2 = $7. $3 is the difference, not the total.

items.q: Kai orders a sushi roll and a juice. How much does it cost?
Charlotte buys an ice block. She pays with a $1 coin. How much change does she get?
items.e: Count on from 70c to $1: 70c + 30c = $1. The change is 30c. 70c is the price, not the change.

items.q: Leo buys a cheese stick. He pays with a $1 coin. How much change does he get?
items.e: Count on from 60c to $1: 60c + 40c = $1. The change is 40c. 60c is the price, not the change.

items.q: Oliver buys a sushi roll. He pays with a $5 note. How much change does he get?
items.e: $4 + $1 = $5. The change is $1. $9 adds the money instead of taking it away.

items.q: Liam buys a sausage roll and a juice. He pays with a $10 note. How much change does he get?
items.e: Cost: $3 + $2 = $5. Count on from $5 to $10: $5. The change is $5. $7 forgets the juice.

items.q: William has 50c. He wants an ice block. How much more money does he need?
items.e: Count on from 50c to 70c: 50c + 20c = 70c. He needs 20c more. 30c is the change from $1.

items.q: Grace has $5. She wants a pie and a juice. Does she have enough?
items.e: Cost: $5 + $2 = $7. $7 is more than $5, so no. $5 + $2 = $7, so she needs $2 more.

items.q: Mia buys 3 apples. How much does she spend?
items.e: 3 lots of 30c: 30c, 60c, 90c. That is 90c. 33c adds 30 and 3. 60c is only 2 apples.

items.q: At the sausage sizzle, a sausage costs $2. Zara buys 4 sausages. How much does she pay?
items.e: Count in 2s: $2, $4, $6, $8. That is $8. $6 adds 2 + 4. $10 would be 5 sausages.

items.q: Harper has $1. How many apples can she buy?
items.e: $1 = 100c. Count in 30s: 30c, 60c, 90c. That is 3 apples, with 10c left. 4 apples would cost 120c, which is too much.

items.q: Amelia buys an apple and popcorn. Noah buys an ice block. Who spends more?
items.e: Amelia: 30c + 50c = 80c. Noah: 70c. 80c is more than 70c, so Amelia spends more.

items.q: Ruby has these coins. She buys an ice block for 70c. How much money is left?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 50c, 70c, 90c. That is 90c. Count on from 70c to 90c: 70c + 20c = 90c. 20c is left. 70c is the cost of the ice block.

items.q: Ethan buys an apple and an ice block. He pays with a $2 coin. How much change does he get?
items.e: Cost: 30c + 70c = 100c = $1. Count on from $1 to $2: $1. The change is $1. $2 is the coin, not the change. 30c is the change from $1 for the ice block only.

items.q: Jack buys 2 sushi rolls. He pays with a $10 note. How much change does he get?
items.e: Cost: $4 + $4 = $8. Count on from $8 to $10: $2. The change is $2. $6 is the change for only 1 sushi roll.

items.q: Ava’s mum puts a $10 note in her lunch order bag. The order is a pie and a juice. How much change comes back?
items.e: Cost: $5 + $2 = $7. Count on from $7 to $10: $3. The change is $3. $7 is the cost, not the change. $5 forgets the juice.

items.q: Matilda and Chloe share a sushi roll. They each pay the same amount. How much does each one pay?
items.e: Share $4 into 2 equal parts: $2 and $2. Each one pays $2. $4 is the whole sushi roll.

items.q: Aarav has these coins. He wants a sausage roll for $3. How much will be left?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: $2, $4, $5. That is $5. Count on from $3 to $5: $2. $2 will be left. $3 is the cost, not what is left. $1 forgets the $1 coin.
